# US tax and reporting for a US person owning foreign rental property

This dimension applies regardless of which country is chosen, plus a per-country
treaty position. Sources in [citations.md](../citations.md).

## The headline: estate tax treaty status, all nine countries

Where no estate tax treaty exists, a US decedent's foreign real property can be
taxed by both jurisdictions on death. The IRS states the exposure in its own
words [51]:

> "An estate of a U.S. citizen or U.S. resident decedent for estate tax purposes
> may face double taxation as a result of the decedent's ownership of foreign
> property because the United States generally taxes the world-wide property of
> a U.S. decedent and the foreign country may tax property situated within such
> foreign country."

The IRS maintains a closed, enumerative list of countries with estate and/or
gift tax treaties [45], corroborated by the Form 706 Schedule P instructions,
which name the countries with "death tax conventions… in effect" [46].

| Country | Estate/death tax treaty | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| **France** | **Yes** — and the only one of the nine with a **gift** tax instrument named | [45][46] |
| **Italy** | **Yes**, estate. Gift position not established | [45][46] |
| **Greece** | **Yes**, estate. Gift position not established | [45][46] |
| Costa Rica | **No** | absent from [45][46] |
| Hungary | **No** | absent from [45][46] |
| Spain | **No** | absent from [45][46] |
| Portugal | **No** | absent from [45][46] |
| Mexico | **No** | absent from [45][46] |
| Panama | **No** | absent from [45][46] |

The absence findings are load-bearing and are stated only because the IRS list
is explicitly enumerative rather than illustrative. **Six of the nine countries
have no estate tax treaty with the United States.** Estate and gift treaties are
distinct instruments; only France is confirmed for both.

### The fallback where no treaty exists

IRC § 2014 gives a unilateral credit for foreign death taxes, and it is narrower
than treaty relief [49]:

- Credit only for taxes "actually paid to any foreign country in respect of any
  property situated within such foreign country and included in the gross
  estate".
- **Two ratio limitations**, one tied to the proportion of foreign-situs taxed
  property, one to the US tax after the § 2010 and § 2012 credits.
- **No credit for interest or penalties** on the foreign tax (26 CFR
  § 20.2014-1(a)).
- The credit is allowed only for taxes paid and claimed **within 4 years** of
  filing the return; refunds are made **without interest**.
- Credit or deduction under § 2053(d)(1), not both [51].

Practically: heirs must complete a foreign probate, pay the foreign tax, obtain
Form 706-CE, and claim within four years, with a separate computation per
country [46].

Where a treaty *does* apply — France, Italy, Greece — the taxpayer may take
whichever is most favourable of the treaty credit, the statutory credit, or the
treaty credit plus the statutory credit for political-subdivision taxes not
covered by the treaty [46]. Treaty positions require disclosure on Form 8833 [51].

## Income tax treaties — a separate question, with one live surprise

Of the nine, the IRS A-to-Z list [50] includes France, Greece, Italy, Mexico,
Portugal and Spain, and carries the verbatim entry:

> "Hungary – CAUTION Treaty Terminated"

No termination date is given on the page. **Costa Rica and Panama do not appear
on the list at all.**

Income tax treaties are not investment-protection instruments and confer no
investor-state recourse. They are listed here because the Hungary termination
directly affects double-tax relief on rental income for one of the nine.

## Reporting — foreign real estate held directly is not reportable

The IRS comparison table is unambiguous [47]:

> "Foreign real estate held directly — [Form 8938:] **No** — [FBAR:] **No**"

But holding through an entity flips it:

> "Foreign real estate held through a foreign entity — No, but the foreign
> entity itself is a specified foreign financial asset and its maximum value
> includes the value of the real estate"

This matters directly for Mexico's restricted-zone trust and for the corporate
structures common in Costa Rica and Panama.

Rental operations normally require a local bank account, and that account is
reportable. FBAR threshold: aggregate value of foreign financial accounts
exceeding **$10,000** at any time in the year, filed with FinCEN separately from
the tax return, due 15 April with an automatic extension to 15 October. Form
8938 thresholds for a specified individual living in the US: **$50,000** at
year-end or **$75,000** at any time, unmarried; $100,000 / $150,000 married
filing jointly; four times those amounts for filers living abroad. The two
regimes are independent — "The Form 8938 filing requirement does not replace or
otherwise affect a taxpayer's obligation to file FinCEN Form 114" [47].

Form 8938 penalties run to $10,000 for failure to disclose plus $10,000 per 30
days after IRS notice, to a maximum of $60,000, with criminal penalties possible
[47].

## Depreciation — the foreign asset is structurally worse

IRC § 168(g)(1)(A) makes the alternative depreciation system **mandatory**, not
elective, for "any tangible property which during the taxable year is used
predominantly outside the United States" [48]. Under § 168(g)(2) the method is
straight line and the recovery period for **residential rental property is 30
years**. The TCJA effective-date note applies the current table to property
placed in service after **31 December 2017** [48].

Domestic residential rental property runs on a **27.5-year** period under
§ 168(c) [48]. Identical property, identical taxpayer: the foreign asset yields a
smaller annual deduction purely because of where it sits.

**A number this document deliberately does not state.** The pre-2018 ADS period
for foreign residential rental property is commonly quoted as 40 years. The
fetched statutory text does **not** state it — the amendment note records that
the old items were struck out without giving their values, and every "40 years"
in § 168 refers to *nonresidential* real property or to § 1245 real property
with no class life [48]. The 40-year figure is therefore unsourced in this run
and is omitted rather than repeated.

Also relevant to a short-let strategy: § 168(e)(2) defines residential rental
property by an **80%-or-more of gross rental income from dwelling units** test
[48], so the characterisation is income-mix dependent.

## Gaps

Two items named in the research brief returned **nothing** in this run, and no
claim is made about either:

- **IRC § 904 foreign tax credit limitation and the passive category.** A
  recursive search of the whole fetched corpus for "foreign tax credit", "passive
  category", "form 1116" and "section 904" returned zero substantive hits. The
  statutory text was fetched late and is not analysed here.
- **IRC § 988 currency gain** on repayment of a foreign-currency mortgage.
  Likewise zero coverage. Do not mistake the currency rules that *are* present —
  Form 706's "rate of exchange in effect at the time each payment of foreign tax
  is made", and the year-end rates used for Form 8938 and FBAR valuation [46][47]
  — for § 988 authority. They are unrelated.
